cards.html: This capstone runs one new request through every skill. Try each step yourself before opening the answer. There is no single right wording; what matters is that each step does its job.

Nadia writes on Monday: "People seem to be quitting the Spanish course. Can you look into it before Thursday's planning meeting?"

What Sam knows: Spanish is Parla's biggest course. Week-4 retention for Spanish learners (the share still doing lessons four weeks after starting) fell from 30% to 26% over the last quarter. In the same quarter, marketing ran a large paid-ads campaign for Spanish in a new region.

Climb the ladder (skill 2), then score your question (skill 3).

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Goal: keep more Spanish learners learning past the first month. Decision: at Thursday's planning, fund a content fix for the Spanish course, or ask marketing to change the campaign's targeting (or both). Metric: Spanish week-4 retention, by sign-up channel and by the lesson where learners stopped, for learners who started last quarter. Hypothesis: part of the drop is the new ad traffic, which retains worse; and a specific early lesson causes extra quitting among all learners. Rejection condition: if retention fell equally in every channel and quitting is spread evenly across lessons, both ideas are wrong. "Which channels and which lessons explain the drop in Spanish week-4 retention this quarter, so we decide between fixing content and changing ad targeting?" scores 3.

Write a short spec (skill 5) and name one guardrail for whatever fix follows (skill 7).

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Numerator: learners who started Spanish in the window and completed at least one lesson in their 4th week. Denominator: learners who started Spanish in the window and completed their first lesson. Window: start dates in the last full quarter. Exclusions: test accounts; learners who switched course (counted separately). Rationale: starting from the first completed lesson ignores people who only browsed. Guardrail: for a content change, Spanish lessons completed per learner must not fall; for a targeting change, new Spanish learners per week must not drop more than an agreed amount.

ChannelRetention beforeShare beforeRetention afterShare after
Organic35%75%35%55%
Paid ads15%25%15%45%

How much of the drop is mix shift? Also: within organic learners, lesson 6 (the past tense) has a 40% quit rate, against about 10% for other lessons, and it was 40% last quarter too. What does that tell you?

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Before: 0.75 × 35% + 0.25 × 15% = 26.25% + 3.75% = 30%. After: 0.55 × 35% + 0.45 × 15% = 19.25% + 6.75% = 26%. The whole 4-point drop is mix shift: neither channel changed. Lesson 6 is a separate, older problem: it didn't cause this quarter's drop, but it is the biggest single leak in the course. Before quoting it, run the volume check (how many learners reach lesson 6?) and look for a confound (did lesson 6 change recently? It didn't).

Write the 3-line recommendation (skill 12) and pick a depth (skill 9).

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Found: the drop in Spanish week-4 retention (30% to 26%) is entirely the new ad traffic, which retains at 15% against 35% for organic learners; neither group got worse. Separately, lesson 6 loses 40% of the learners who reach it, four times the usual rate. Means: the content didn't get worse, so a rewrite won't fix the headline; but lesson 6 is the biggest leak in our biggest course. Do: (1) ask marketing to judge the campaign on week-4 learners, not sign-ups; (2) split lesson 6 into two shorter lessons, about a week of content work. If 20,000 learners a quarter reach it, cutting the quit rate from 40% to 25% keeps about 3,000 more of them. The depth is an initial exploration that answered the question; no deep dive is needed for a one-week content change.

Write the decision-time half of the checklist (skill 13).

🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

Decision: split lesson 6; marketing reports week-4 learners per dollar. Target: lesson 6 quit rate from 40% to 25% within 30 days of release. Follow-up: 30 days after release, measured outside any promotion, with the channel split held constant so a mix shift can't fake a win. Owner: Sam. Then share the result with Nadia and marketing, and take the next, sharper question back to step 1.

quiz.q: Nadia: 'People seem to be quitting the Spanish course.' First move?
o: Climb the ladder: goal and decision first

quiz.q: Before: 75% organic at 35% and 25% paid at 15%. Week-4 retention in %?
After: 55% organic at 35% and 45% paid at 15%. Week-4 retention in %?
Neither channel's retention changed. What explains the drop?
quiz.why: The share of lower-retention paid learners grew.

quiz.q: Lesson 6 has a 40% quit rate, and had it last quarter too. What is it?
o: The cause of this quarter's drop
A separate, older leak worth fixing
quiz.why: It didn't cause the drop, but it's the biggest leak.

quiz.q: 20,000 learners reach lesson 6. Quit rate falls from 40% to 25%. How many more learners stay?
Which guardrail fits a targeting change for the Spanish ads?
o: New Spanish learners per week mustn't drop past an agreed amount
quiz.why: Better targeting may bring fewer, better learners; agree the limit first.

quiz.q: When should the follow-up be measured?
o: 30 days after release, outside promotions, channel mix held constant
quiz.why: A clean window, so neither a sale nor a mix shift can fake a win.

quiz.q: Since the drop is all mix shift, there's nothing for the content team to do.
quiz.why: Myth. Lesson 6 is still the biggest leak in the biggest course.

quiz.q: Which depth did the Spanish question need?
o: An initial exploration that answered it
quiz.why: It answered the decision; a one-week content change needs no deep dive.
